decisions.q: Which layout should the lead list use?
decisions.ctx: People skim 30–50 leads a day and open only a few of them to reply.
decisions.pattern: When the options are screen designs. Show the designs side by side and line up the rows so differences read across.

dims.q: How many leads fit on one screen?
How many moves until you reply?
Does it work on a phone?
What changes, and what do you check?

options.label: Table

notes.text: The right columns are cut off on a phone

d.v: Reuses the table component · check 1 screen
d.why: The same table is already used elsewhere

options.when: Skimming many leads quickly matters most
options.gist: Best for skimming many, awkward on a phone
options.give: You leave the list every time you reply
options.means: Leads appear as dense rows, and clicking a name opens a separate detail page. After replying you have to go back to the list.
after: Clicking a name opens a detail page
options.lens: Easy to add columns → in a few months the table may get too wide
options.example: On her laptop, Mina sees 12 leads at once; to reply she opens the detail page.

detail.prereq: The detail page is a separate screen, so after going back you have to find your place in the list again.
detail.confusion: "A table is fastest" is only true for skimming. Counting the reply, it is slower.

options.label: List + detail
options.cap: Pick on the left, see it on the right

d.v: New layout + moving the reply box · check 2 screens and the reply flow
d.why: The reply box has never been moved; sending could break

options.when: Fits skimming and then replying right away
options.gist: Skim and reply right away, but fewer leads at once
options.flaw: It shows 4 fewer leads than the table, and on a narrow screen the detail feels cramped.
options.means: Clicking someone on the left opens their details and a reply box on the right. You can reply without leaving the list, but only 8 people fit at once.
after: List on the left, detail on the right
options.lens: Adds a detail area → room later for notes and conversation history
options.example: Mina clicks someone on the left and their details and a reply box open on the right.
options.check: After sending a reply, the list stays scrolled where it was
options.next: Build the split layout and put the reply box in the detail

evidence: How much moving the reply box touches is estimated from a similar screen
detail.prereq: "Detail" is the right-hand area with one person's information and a reply box.
detail.confusion: On a phone the list and the detail become two screens. They do not sit side by side there.

panels.caption: 1. In the morning the list shows 8 people
2. Clicking one opens the detail on the right
3. Reply, then click the next person

options.label: Cards

notes.text: One per row on a phone, as is

d.v: New card component · check 1 screen and a phone
d.why: A similar card screen was built before

options.when: There is a lot to show, like photos and notes
options.gist: Easiest on a phone, slow for skimming many
options.means: Each person gets one card. It is comfortable on a phone, but even on a laptop only 6 people show at once.
options.lens: Easy to add photos and tags → cards grow and fewer fit over time
options.example: On her phone Mina scrolls one card at a time; on a laptop she sees 6.
options.check: Cards are not cut off at a 375px phone width

decisions.same: All three keep the same search, filter and sort.
decisions.plain: The lead list is the screen where every new inquiry shows up as a line. You are choosing whether it looks like a dense table, a list on the left with details on the right, or one card per person. The shape changes how many people you see at once and how easy it is to reply.
decisions.stake: The basic frame of a screen you skim 30–50 times a day

undo.how: Only the screen code changes; the data stays

recNote.if: skimming and then replying right away matters most
recNote.why: It is the only one where you never leave the list to reply.

decisions.q: What should the sign-up button say?
decisions.ctx: It is the last button of the free-trial form. See each one placed on a real button.
decisions.pattern: Copy is not judged as plain text. Show it in the place it will actually appear.

options.label: Sign up
options.when: The text above the form already explains enough
options.gist: If nothing changes: unclear what you sign up for
options.means: The button keeps saying "Sign up". Nothing changes.

options.label: Start free
options.when: Easing payment worries is the point
options.gist: Least pressure, but the trial length is hidden
options.means: The button changes to "Start free". Visitors see right away that it costs nothing, but the button does not say how many days the trial lasts.
options.check: Compare sign-ups with today's for two weeks

options.label: Finish sign-up in 3 minutes
d: 27 characters · cut off on narrow screens
options.when: The form looks long and people drop off
options.gist: Promises speed, cut off on phones
options.give: Short length, and a promise you may not keep
options.means: The button changes to "Finish sign-up in 3 minutes". It promises speed, so sign-up really has to take under 3 minutes.

decisions.plain: You are choosing the words on the button at the bottom of the sign-up form. It is the last thing a visitor reads before deciding whether to press it. It should be short and still say what happens when you press it.
decisions.stake: The last button of the sign-up form; every visitor sees it

recNote.if: making the first click feel safe matters most
recNote.why: It says "free" and fits on one line on a phone.

decisions.q: What unit should site permissions use?
decisions.ctx: Today, permission keys differ per menu inside the same group, so three places are out of sync.
decisions.more: The three places are SEO, images and channels. In each, the group's permission and the menu's permission key were set separately.
decisions.pattern: Draw structure you can't see by its size and shape. Here, the number of cells to manage is drawn as is.

dims.q: Does the database have to change?
Can the same problem happen again?
What changes, and what do you check?

options.label: 6 groups × view/edit
options.when: You want it simple and the mismatches gone
options.gist: Simple, and the mismatch cannot return
options.give: Blocking one single menu on its own
options.means: Access is split into 6 groups, each with view and edit. Every menu follows the group it belongs to.
options.check: The 3 mismatched menus now get the right access
options.next: Define the 6 groups and attach menus to them

options.label: 29 menus × view/edit/send
d: New permission table and a move · check all 29 menus
options.when: People need different access per menu

undo.how: Drop the new table and go back to the old keys

options.give: Simplicity, and a lot of checking
options.means: Each of the 29 menus gets its own view, edit and send. It is precise, but admins manage 87 cells.

options.label: Keep the 4 keys, fix only the mismatches
options.when: You only need to put out the urgent fire
options.gist: Puts out the fire, but it can happen again
options.give: Any guarantee it stays in sync
options.means: The 4 keys stay as they are and only the 3 mismatched menus are fixed. When menus are added, they can drift again.

decisions.plain: You are choosing how to split what each site admin can see and change. Give access in a few big groups, split it per menu, or patch what exists today. Finer splits are more precise but leave more to manage.
decisions.stake: The unit of admin access; tedious to change later

undo.how: The permission table has to be moved again

recNote.if: you want it simple and the mismatches gone
recNote.why: When menus follow their group, the same problem cannot come back.

visual.legend: Inner: reads permissions directly · outer: uses the result · dotted: not checked

decisions.q: How far should the work branch go?
decisions.ctx: Pushing is hard to undo, so we ask before doing it.
decisions.pattern: A check before a hard-to-undo action. Current state as number chips; options drawn as how far it goes.

options.label: Up to staging
d: One more step to production after checking
options.when: You want to look at it before it goes out
options.gist: One more look before users see it
options.give: Users see it about a day later
options.means: The code goes to the staging server only. Users cannot see it yet; after checking, it goes to production in a second step.
options.check: The new list screen opens on staging
options.next: Ask again about production once it checks out

options.label: Straight to production

undo.how: Deploy again; until then users see the changed screen

options.gist: Live right away; users see any mistake first
options.give: The chance to check before users see it
options.means: The code goes straight to production. Users see it today, and if something is wrong they see it until it is deployed again.
options.check: Error logs do not rise in the 10 minutes after deploying

options.label: Don't push yet
d: Commits pile up and get harder to merge
options.when: You'll push once the work in progress is done
options.gist: If nothing changes: harder to merge later
options.give: A chance to check these changes
options.means: Nothing goes to any server. It all goes up together once the work in progress is done.

decisions.plain: You are choosing how far the finished code goes. Staging is a practice server only we can see; production is the server real users use. Once it is on production, users see it right away, and undoing it means deploying again.
decisions.stake: On production, users see it right away

recNote.if: you want one more look before users see it
recNote.why: Staging is invisible to users and easy to roll back.

terms: a server for checking that real users cannot see

panels.title: If it goes wrong, the likeliest reason
panels.text: Production settings differ from staging, so the new screen could show an empty list. Staging could not check this.

decisions.q: Which accent color should we use?
decisions.ctx: It is used on buttons, links, badges and charts. Hover an option to change the preview.
decisions.pattern: For choices that change the overall feel: colors, fonts, spacing. One big preview, with the options swapped in.

options.label: Indigo
options.means: Buttons and links turn indigo. It feels calm, and white text on buttons reads well.

options.label: Green
options.means: Buttons and links turn green. It feels relaxed.

options.label: Orange
options.means: Buttons and links turn orange. It stands out, but white text on buttons may be less crisp.

decisions.plain: You are choosing the main color for buttons and highlights across the app. The color changes how the service feels, and whether white text on a button is easy to read.
decisions.stake: The color on buttons, links and badges

decisions.q: Pick what goes into this week.
decisions.ctx: The numbers are how many screens you will need to check this week. You can check up to 5. A recommended set is laid out.
decisions.pattern: A pick-several decision. The total changes as you choose, so you can see when it overflows.

items.label: Forms admin
items.sub: Create and edit forms without code

items.label: Auto DM
items.sub: Reply automatically to people who comment

decisions.plain: You are choosing what gets built this week. Only what you pick is built now; the rest waits. There is a limit to how much you can check in a week, so not everything fits.
decisions.stake: What gets built this week and what waits

decisions.ctx: Any of them is easy to change later. You can accept the recommendations in one go.
decisions.pattern: When there are several light decisions. One row each, and a way to finish them all with the recommendations.
decisions.plain: Five small behaviors around the screens. Each is light and easy to change later. You can take all the recommendations in one go and change only the ones you disagree with.
decisions.stake: Small behaviors that are easy to change later

decisions.q: How many auto DMs should go out per day?
decisions.ctx: 1,200 people are waiting for a reply. Sending more finishes sooner but raises the risk of an account restriction.
decisions.pattern: For picking a number. Move the value and the results change, so you can see where it is reasonable.

stops.label: Recommended
stops.means: At 200 a day everyone is reached in 6 days. About 3 times in 100, the account may be blocked for a day.

outs.why: Never sent more than 400 a day, so this is an estimate.
Never sent more than 400 a day, so this is an estimate.

decisions.plain: You are choosing how many automatic DMs go out per day. Sending more finishes sooner, but Instagram may treat it as spam and briefly block the account. It is a choice between finishing fast and keeping the account safe.
decisions.stake: Finishing fast against keeping the account safe

undo.how: You can change the daily number while sending. DMs already sent cannot be taken back.

recNote.if: finishing fast and account safety matter about the same
recNote.why: 200 a day is what was sent over the last 3 months without a restriction.

decisions.depends: If auto DM is left out of the scope in question 6, this one is not needed.
decisions.assume: Assumes 1,200 people. The chance of a block is estimated from the last 3 months of sending and Instagram's guidance.

themes.label: Seen by users
themes.desc: What leads or visitors see themselves

themes.label: Undo
themes.desc: Whether you can go back after a wrong choice

themes.label: Speed vs safety
themes.desc: Finishing sooner against making fewer mistakes
